theme: Moses’ psalm, God’s eternity against human frailty
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 90. It is the only psalm attributed to Moses. Read it as a reflection by a man who has led a rebellious people for forty years and knows both God’s eternity and human weakness.
settingTheScene: Psalm 90 opens the fourth book of the Psalms. The title is “A Prayer of Moses, the man of God.” If Moses wrote it, it comes from the wilderness years, when a whole generation died without entering the promised land. The sense of time passing, of lives cut short, and of God’s anger against sin runs through it. It is placed here as a companion to the book of Numbers.
observation: “Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations” (v. 1).
“Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God” (v. 2).
“You return man to dust and say, Return, O children of man!” (v. 3).
“For a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, or as a watch in the night” (v. 4).
“The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty” (v. 10).
“So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom” (v. 12).
“Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days” (v. 14).
“Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!” (v. 17).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a surprising claim for a people with no home: “You have been our dwelling place.” Israel had no land and lived in tents. But Moses says that their true home was never a place. It was God. This is the first sentence of the psalm, and everything else depends on it.

Then comes a contrast between God’s eternity and human frailty. God is from everlasting to everlasting. We are like grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening. Moses does not say this to make us feel hopeless. He says it so that we see how much we depend on God.

The cause of our frailty is not only that we are creatures. It is that we are sinners. Verses 7 to 11 connect human mortality to God’s anger. “We are brought to an end by your anger.” Moses had watched a generation die in the wilderness because of unbelief, and he knows that death is not natural. It is a sign of judgment. Our secret sins are “in the light of your presence.”

But the psalm does not end with despair. It turns in verse 12, with a prayer: “Teach us to number our days.” The right response to our short lives is wisdom, living each day with an awareness of its limits. Then it asks for compassion: “Have pity on your servants.” It asks for joy in the morning, joy to match the years of affliction. And it ends with a request that the work of our hands might be established. God’s favor is what makes small and brief work last.

It is a good psalm to read at the start of a long book about the wilderness. It reminds us that the journey is brief, that God is our home, and that his steadfast love is the only thing that satisfies.
connection: Peter quotes verse 4 when he says that “with the Lord one day is as a thousand years” (2 Peter 3:8). James says that life is “a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes” (James 4:14). Paul teaches that death entered through sin and that Christ has defeated it (Romans 5:12; 1 Corinthians 15:54-57). Jesus said that in his Father’s house there are many rooms (John 14:2), and he is our dwelling place now.
application:
Ask yourself how many days you may have left, and what you most want to do with them. Pray verse 12 for yourself.

Think about the work you are doing right now. Ask God to establish it, and to make it last for his purposes.

Thank God that he is your dwelling place, even when you feel like a wanderer.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for being your dwelling place in every season of life.
Ask him to teach you to number your days and gain a heart of wisdom.
Ask him to establish the work of your hands for his glory.
